summary: Discovery call covering PrismShore's latency (p95) and throughput goals across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployment options. Key constraints: sub-300ms p95 first-token for chat-like queries, sustained peak of ~10k aggregate tokens/sec during daytime surge, strict data residency and SOC2 needs. Redwood AE/SE discussed batch/caching/quantization levers, dedicated pool sizing, and pilot steps. Agreed next steps: benchmark run, pricing deck, and security docs.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) decision factors
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya with Redwood Inference, AE on the account. We invited Ethan, our systems SE, to run through latency and throughput stuff. How're you all doing?
[00:00:06] Raj Patel: Doing well, Maya. Thanks. I'm Raj, CTO at PrismShore. We brought Lena and Sofia to cover infra and model details.
[00:00:12] Lena Ortiz: Hi all. Quick note we had a hard stop at 5:00pm PT.
[00:00:15] Maya Chen: Great, we'll keep it tight. Quick agenda: understand target p95s, concurrency patterns, streaming expectations, and then deployment mode tradeoffs — hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC. Ethan will go deep on performance levers.
[00:00:30] Ethan Park: Hi — Ethan, hi. I'll try not to drown you in numbers but wanted to map their workload to realistic token/sec and latency profiles.
[00:00:36] Sofia Gomez: Thanks. For context our product does live summarization and assisted triage. Typical request sizes 30-80 tokens in prompt, completions 16-64 tokens. Our biggest ask: first-token p95 under 300ms for interactive flows, ideally <200ms. During peak marketing hours we get sudden spikes — day peaks with roughly 600 concurrent active users, average session 1.2 requests/sec, but bursts can be heavier.
[00:01:00] Maya Chen: Good concrete numbers. Do you currently host models yourself or use external APIs?
[00:01:04] Raj Patel: We're currently on a mixed setup — some in-house inference for embedding-ish workloads and OpenAI for generative chat. We're evaluating moving more to hosted/dedicated because costs and latency are unpredictable.
[00:01:16] Ethan Park: When you say unpredictable, is it both latency spikes and token cost?
[00:01:20] Raj Patel: Yeah. Also need clearer routing for failover — we can't depend on a single external endpoint during promos.
[00:01:26] Lena Ortiz: Also important: must not leak PII outside our VPC. So the private option or dedicated with strong network isolation and KMS integration is a must to evaluate.
[00:01:35] Maya Chen: Understood. On p95, let's be explicit: first-token latency target 200–300ms. Is that end-to-end including network from client to our edge?
[00:01:44] Sofia Gomez: It needs to be end-to-end. We measure from the user's browser event, so network counts. Typical region is us-west-2.
[00:01:50] Ethan Park: Okay that matters. For hosted we can edge terminate close to region; for private on-prem you'll need a tiny edge or a dedicated proxy. Big lever is model selection + quantization. For example, fp16 Llama-2-13B on a gpus with 48GB might give first-token ~120–180ms in ideal conditions for short sequences, but depends on software path. q4_8 (4-bit quant) can push throughput higher but first-token sometimes increases a bit due to dequant/comp overhead depending on kernel.
[00:02:18] Raj Patel: Our team is leaning toward 13B family sized models for cost reasons. We want to run an internal eval but need a partner that can guarantee p95 SLOs or at least predictable behavior.
[00:02:28] Ethan Park: Makes sense. For 13B class, dedicated pools with tuning (batching, KV cache, persistent warm pool) usually hit 200–300ms p95 for 1–2 token streaming starts. If you need <200ms reliably at 600 concurrency, you'd want reserved capacity — a Dedicated cluster with autoscaling buffer and burst nodes.
[00:02:43] Maya Chen: Also mention prefix caching: if many requests share a common system prompt or prefix, KV/prefix caching can collapse repeated compute and drastically reduce tail latency. Is your workload shareable like that?
[00:02:52] Sofia Gomez: Yes, ~40% of sessions share a near-identical prompt template, so caching would help.
[00:02:57] Ethan Park: That helps a lot. With prefix caching plus reasonable batching we can reduce aggregate GPU tokens/sec load by 20–40% on some workloads. Batching is a particularly big cost win, but it increases latency for single-user spikes if you set batch windows too long. Redwood's runtime does continuous batching with per-queue latency SLOs — you can cap max batching delay to keep p95 in target.
[00:03:18] Lena Ortiz: Important for us: we cannot have batching introduce >50ms additional delay for interactive flows.
[00:03:23] Ethan Park: Totally doable — you can configure max batch delay to 10–30ms; most deployments use 20ms to balance throughput.
[00:03:30] Raj Patel: Can you walk through a sizing example? If we want p95 first-token <250ms, 600 concurrent, median response ~40 tokens, peak aggregate token/sec target is roughly?
[00:03:40] Ethan Park: Quick back-of-envelope: 600 concurrent * 1.2 req/sec * avg 40 tokens = 28,800 tokens/sec aggregate. But that's worst-case if all requests require full generation simultaneously. With prefix caching reducing repeated work by 30–40% and with batching efficiency, the realistic tokens/sec to serve might drop into 15k–20k tokens/sec. Quantization to q4_8 can increase throughput similarly. Dedicated cluster sizing: for 13B q4_8 you might need 6–8 A100-ish equivalents to sustain a steady 20k tokens/sec with good p95 coverage, depending on kernel efficiency. For fp16 you'd need more. We'll run benchmarks to produce precise numbers.
[00:04:14] Maya Chen: Worth noting, those A100 numbers are rough — Ethan will demo baseline runs. Also routing: Redwood can route by latency-first (pin to region), cost-first, or fall back to a cheaper model if capacity constrained. That reduces the need for extreme reserve capacity but it's a tradeoff for output quality.
[00:04:30] Sofia Gomez: We can't afford much quality drop on triage flows. Maybe we can allow fallback for non-critical endpoints (summaries of long docs) but triage chat needs top quality.
[00:04:40] Ethan Park: Right, you can have route policies per endpoint. Also multi-variant models: keep a higher quality 13B fp16 pinned for triage, and a quantized 7B or 13B q4_8 for non-critical.
[00:04:51] Raj Patel: On the private side, what's the overhead for on-prem? We have an air-gapped-ish data center in us-west and prefer VPC if possible.
[00:04:59] Ethan Park: For Private (VPC or on-prem), initial setup includes control-plane peering, network firewall rules, and KMS/HSM integration. Latency-wise, on-prem can be very good inside your network but you'll need to deploy a lightweight edge or colocate model servers to avoid internet hops. The Redwood private package can run in your VPC with customer-managed networking; we support bringing-your-own-kms and audit logs.
[00:05:18] Lena Ortiz: SOC2 compliance: Do you have SOC2 docs readily shareable? Also retention/ephemeral logs?
[00:05:22] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll share SOC2 and our standard compliance pack. For audit logs you can configure retention and anonymization; Private gives you more control.
[00:05:30] Raj Patel: Cost is key. Can you give an expected monthly spend range for Dedicated vs Hosted for our scenario?
[00:05:36] Maya Chen: We'll put exact numbers in the pricing deck, but high level: Hosted is lower entry friction but per-token cost is higher and variability remains. Dedicated with reserved capacity amortizes GPU cost and gives predictable unit economics; you'll pay base reserved + overage for bursts or autoscale. For your 15k–20k tokens/sec steady-state, Dedicated likely saves 30–50% over Hosted at scale, but needs commit.
[00:05:56] Sofia Gomez: If we do a 2-week pilot, can we test both Hosted baseline and a small Dedicated pool?
[00:06:02] Ethan Park: Yes. We typically do a pilot with a dedicated test cluster sized to your expected steady-state and run token/sec/latency profiles using your traces. We'll also test with and without prefix caching and with q4_8 vs fp16.
[00:06:15] Raj Patel: What's the timeline? We have a product launch in mid-December so ideally production by early December.
[00:06:21] Maya Chen: Tight but doable. Pilot week of Nov 3rd (you requested) — if benchmarks look good we can fast-track procurement for a December rollout.
[00:06:29] Lena Ortiz: Regarding network peering — we have strict egress rules; will Redwood need peering or can we route via a proxy?
[00:06:36] Ethan Park: Options: 1) VPC peering for Private, 2) dedicated IP allowlist for Hosted with TLS and mutual auth, 3) edge proxy in your network that talks to Redwood. We'll document all three and recommend based on latency and compliance.
[00:06:47] Sofia Gomez: One more: streaming behavior. We stream token-by-token to the browser; first-token latency is critical but also steady token cadence must be smooth. Do you throttle or batch streaming differently?
[00:06:57] Ethan Park: Streaming is handled by the runtime — we emit tokens as soon as they're generated. Continuous batching usually groups in the decoder path but streaming shaves off immediate tokens; for steady cadence we ensure the generator path isn't starved. There is some tradeoff: high batching for throughput can increase jitter in token timing, but the runtime has burst queues so you can have a low-latency streaming path with slightly lower batch efficiency.
[00:07:19] Raj Patel: Any gotchas?
[00:07:21] Maya Chen: Watch cold starts: if your pool scales to zero, first requests will see higher latency. For Dedicated we keep a warm baseline and you can allocate burst nodes. Also be mindful of quantization regression; we can run evals against your prompt set.
[00:07:34] Ethan Park: I'll add that tokenization differences (your tokenizer vs model tokenization) can change token counts; share a sample so we benchmark realistic token/sec.
[00:07:42] Lena Ortiz: We'll send traces and a couple dozen representative prompts.
[00:07:45] Maya Chen: Great. Quick recap of next steps: Ethan runs the baseline perf tests on their traces, Maya sends pricing and compliance docs, PrismShore sends traces and infra diagram, and we schedule pilot the week of Nov 3.
[00:07:59] Raj Patel: Sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[00:08:03] Ethan Park: No blockers. We'll need the traces and a p95 matrix to make the benchmark targeted.
[00:08:08] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with a calendar invite and links to the SOC2 packet.
[00:08:13] Sofia Gomez: Appreciate it.
[00:08:15] [Call ends with quick handshake and some small talk about holiday schedules; transcript has a few mis-attributions where the automated speaker tag changed mid-sentence.]

Notes on transcription: speaker tags occasionally flip (Ethan sometimes labelled Speaker 2), minor mis-hearings: q4_8 transcribed as "q-four-eight" in places, KV cache sometimes as "K Vcache". Some timestamps rounded to nearest 5–10s.

Benchmarks / technical takeaways:
- Target p95 first-token <250ms (end-to-end) with 600 concurrent peak; realistic aggregate tokens/sec estimate 15k–20k after caching and batching.
- Dedicated pool recommendation: reserved 6–8 A100-ish equivalents for q4_8 13B variant; pilot cluster smaller for benchmark.
- Levers: prefix/KV caching (~30–40% effective), continuous batching (with 10–30ms max delay), quantization (q4_8) for throughput, and model routing/fallbacks for non-critical endpoints.
